stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his father, who works as a hospital orderly, after about three weeks of intermittent abdominal pain, low-grade fevers, and reduced appetite. His mother initially thought it was a recurring stomach bug going around the neighborhood. He has become noticeably less active. No known TB contact in the household, though the family lives in a densely populated building. No prior TB treatment, no known drug-resistant contact. Abdominal ultrasound shows mesenteric lymphadenopathy with a small amount of free fluid. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of a mesenteric node was performed and sent for molecular testing, which was positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, no guarding, no palpable mass, no peripheral lymphadenopathy.

patient.occupation: not applicable (household occupational context: father works as a hospital orderly)
patient.social_history: Lives with parents in a densely populated residential building
patient.presenting_complaint: Intermittent abdominal pain, low-grade fevers, reduced appetite, reduced activity
patient.exam_findings: Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, no guarding, no palpable mass, mesenteric lymphadenopathy with free fluid on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever

distractors: A recurring viral gastrointestinal illness circulating in the neighborhood proposed as the explanation for the abdominal pain
Reduced activity and appetite attributed to ordinary childhood fussiness rather than a persistent process
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the mesenteric node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the mesenteric node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the abdominal findings entirely to a self-limited viral illness and deferring molecular testing on the aspirate already obtained
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
